chapter_en: Tza'ar Ba'alei Ḥayim (The Suffering of Animals)

sections.body_en:
It is a mitzva to treat animals with compassion and fairness, and it is forbidden to cause them suffering. At the same time, a person is permitted to use animals for his work, as people were accustomed to load burdens on donkeys and mules, to plow with oxen and donkeys, to ride on horses, camels and donkeys, and even to eat the meat of animals. Not only that, but there is a mitzva to offer sacrifices of animals and birds, including also the mitzvot of the scapegoat (se'ir ha-mishtale'aḥ) and the eglah arufah (the calf whose neck is broken). This is what the Sages said, that animals were created to serve man (Kiddushin 82a; Sanhedrin 108a) – and this includes also eating their meat. One could say that just as animals are permitted to eat from plants, so man may eat from animals.

Thus, one must balance between the two values: on the one hand, the needs of man take precedence over the needs of animals, and on the other hand, one must try as much as possible not to cause suffering to animals. Therefore, for example, even when the descendants of Noaḥ were permitted to eat meat, the Torah commanded that they not act cruelly toward animals by eating ever min ha-ḥai (a limb from a living animal).

In practice, when there is a conflict between the needs of man and the aim of not causing suffering to animals, one must weigh the degree of necessity for man against the suffering caused to the animal. For example, eating meat is very important for man, and sheḥita causes the animals only slight suffering (below 18:3), and therefore it is permitted to slaughter animals in order to eat their meat. But when it concerns a less vital need for man, or when the human need causes animals great suffering, the question is more complex. In general, the halakhic decision is determined by weighing three basic principles:

The first rule: there are different levels of suffering: slight suffering, ordinary suffering, great suffering and terrible suffering. The greater the suffering, the more severe the matter, and only rarely, for a most vital need, is one lenient about it.

The second rule: animals are divided into different types, and the more developed the species, the more suffering it feels, and consequently the more careful one must be not to cause it suffering. The level of development is measured by the brain and nervous system. In mammals such as dogs, cattle, monkeys and dolphins, these systems are relatively developed, and therefore one can discern in them feelings of sorrow and joy, and one can even teach them certain things, and the mother recognizes her offspring and cares for them with compassion. There are also differences among the mammalian species; for example, a dog is more developed than a sheep, and therefore it is more capable of expressing certain emotions, and when it is made to suffer its suffering is greater. Below the mammal family are the birds, and below them the reptiles such as lizards, and below them the fish, which generally do not care for their offspring, so that a few minutes after the female fish spawns her small fry she can devour many of them without pangs of conscience. Below the fish are the insects.

The third rule: the more an animal helps man, the more one must treat it with compassion and fairness. Therefore the Torah commanded to help a donkey that has collapsed under its burden (below, section 2), and not to muzzle an animal from eating of the produce with which it works (below, section 3). Therefore, it is more proper to have compassion on domesticated animals, such as the cow, goat, sheep and chickens; likewise dogs, which help in guarding, and cats, which rid the house of snakes and mice.

In summary: le-khatḥila (ideally), one should not cause suffering to any animal, even the lowliest, as it is stated (Tehillim 145:9): "And His compassion is over all His works" (see Bava Metzia 85a). But when a person needs to cause suffering to animals, each case must be weighed according to the three rules mentioned.1

notes_en.en:
Bava Metzia 32b: according to the Sages and Rabbi Shimon, tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim (causing suffering to animals) is a Torah prohibition, and according to Rabbi Yosi Ha-gelili it is rabbinic. This is also the view of Rabban Gamliel in Shabbat 154b. However, in Shabbat 128b it is cited as an accepted view that tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim is a Torah prohibition. This is also the view of the overwhelming majority of poskim, among them: Rif, Ramban, Maharam of Rothenburg, Rashba, Rosh, Meiri, Ḥinukh, Tur and Rema (ḤM 272:9). The main source for this is the mitzva of unloading the donkey (below, halakha 2), and according to the Meiri (Bava Metzia 32b) also the prohibition of "do not muzzle" (halakha 3). However, regarding the view of the Rambam in Hilkhot Rotze'aḥ 13:9 there is perplexity: most commentators hold that according to him the prohibition is rabbinic, but according to the Radbaz and Kesef Mishneh, according to him too the prohibition is from the Torah. Three rules define the prohibition and its severity.
The first rule: there is a distinction between levels of pain, as we learned in Shabbat 128b that because tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim is a Torah prohibition, they permitted rabbinic prohibitions, but the permission is on condition that it is great suffering. So wrote the Nimukei Yosef on Bava Metzia 32b, and the Ḥiddushei Anshei Shem on the Mordekhai (Bava Metzia ch. 2, os 40), that one who causes an animal great suffering transgresses a Torah prohibition, and one who causes slight suffering transgresses a rabbinic prohibition. So too wrote the Ritva and Tosafot Ha-Rosh on Bava Metzia 31a, that the mitzva of unloading a donkey is from the Torah because of tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim, whereas loading it is from the Torah only because of helping one's fellow; even though his helping with the loading removes some suffering from the animal, the removal of slight suffering is not a Torah obligation.
The second rule: since the mitzva is not to cause suffering, it is consequently clear that there is a difference between lower animals that feel less suffering and developed animals that feel more suffering. Indeed, we find that one of the reasons for the sheḥita of domestic and wild animals is so as not to cause them suffering, and for birds, which are less developed, cutting one siman suffices, and fish and locusts, which are at a lower level, do not require sheḥita and the prohibition of ever min ha-ḥai does not apply to them (Radbaz, Metzudat David 202; above 14:6; and below 17:7-8). Similarly, the She'ilat Ya'avetz (1:110) wrote that there is no prohibition of tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim regarding species of insects, but it is a midat ḥasidut (an attribute of piety) not to harm any living thing unnecessarily. And for a need it is permitted even to kill weasels that disturb a person, and the reproach directed at Rabbi (Bava Metzia 85a) was according to his level of piety (below 18:3).
The third rule: the main severity of the prohibition applies to animals that help man, such as a donkey carrying a load and an ox threshing; likewise the halakha that one must provide for the food of animals (below, halakha 4) refers to those that help man, such as cattle for meat and milk and birds for meat and eggs. So wrote the She'ilat Ya'avetz (1:110), and he added that the Torah mitzva also applies to dogs that help guard the house and cats that rid it of snakes and scorpions. End quote. To a lesser degree, there is a mitzva to feed ownerless animals, and if they are hungry one may exert oneself for this on Shabbat (below, halakha 15; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 324:2-3; MB 31).

sections.title_en: Unloading the Donkey – Tza'ar Ba'alei Ḥayim Is a Torah Prohibition
sections.body_en:
There is a Torah mitzva to have compassion on animals and not to cause them suffering, and therefore one who sees a donkey that has collapsed under the weight of its burden is commanded to help unload its burden so that it can get up, as it is stated (Shemot 23:5): "If you see the donkey of one who hates you lying under its burden, and you would refrain from helping him, you shall surely help with him." That is, if you see the donkey of your enemy lying under its burden, and you wish not to help him, strengthen yourself in the mitzva and help him. There are two reasons for this: first, one should not refrain from offering help to a person with whom we are in a dispute; second, to prevent suffering to the donkey that has collapsed under its heavy burden (Bava Metzia 32b).

Since unloading the donkey also includes the mitzva of 'tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim,' when a person asks for help unloading his donkey, one must help him free of charge in order to save his donkey from suffering. But when he asks for help loading his donkey, there is no obligation to help him without payment, just as with all types of work there is no obligation to help him free of charge. When a person needs to stop his work in order to help unload a donkey, he may demand payment for the loss he incurs from stopping his work (Rosh; Rema ḤM 272:6; Sma 9). Some say that since this concerns tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim, even if he will not receive compensation, he is obligated to stop his work in order to save the donkey from its suffering (Ran).

Since one of the purposes of the mitzva is to prevent suffering to the donkey, the mitzva of unloading takes precedence over the mitzva of loading. That is, when two fellows with donkeys need help, one with loading the burden and one with unloading the burden that has made the donkey collapse, one should first help with unloading the burden in order to ease the donkey's suffering. However, if the donkey needing loading belongs to a person with whom one is in a dispute that has reached hatred, one should first help load the enemy's donkey, in order thereby to subdue the evil inclination that brought them to hatred, so that perhaps as a result they will merit to return to loving one another (Bava Metzia 32b; SA ḤM 272:10).

If the one who saw the donkey lying under its burden is a distinguished person who is not accustomed to unloading donkeys in the street, he is not obligated to help unload the donkey, because his dignity is more important, and there is no mitzva for him to demean himself in order to prevent suffering to the donkey. Nevertheless, if he forgoes his dignity and helps the donkey, he fulfills a mitzva. However, a Torah scholar with a public position is forbidden to help unload the donkey, because his dignity is the dignity of the Torah, and he is forbidden to behave in a way that would harm the dignity of the Torah. If he wishes to help, he should hire another person to help the donkey (Rosh, Rema; Arukh Ha-shulḥan ḤM 263:4). Some say that a Torah scholar who conducts himself with the practices of piety and is not concerned for his dignity is permitted to help unload the donkey (Rambam and SA 272:3).

Sefer Ḥasidim (44, 666, 668) wrote that those who cause suffering to their donkey by loading burdens beyond its strength, and afterwards, when it cannot walk, beat it, as well as those who ride horses and hurt them excessively with their boots, will in the future be judged for this. But to strike the animal a little so that it will walk is permitted, for this is how one spurs it on to its work. Indeed, we find that the Holy One, blessed be He, was angered at Bil'am, who struck his donkey for no reason, as it is stated (Bemidbar 22:32): "Why have you struck your donkey?" For since Bil'am knew his donkey, that it always obeyed him, he should not have struck it after it lay down, for he should have understood that there was probably something blocking it from continuing to walk. And since he behaved cruelly, and threatened it: "If there were a sword in my hand, I would now have killed you" – he was punished measure for measure and was killed by the sword.

sections.title_en: "Do Not Muzzle" – The Attitude Toward Working Animals
sections.body_en:
There is a Torah mitzva not to prevent an animal from eating of the produce with which it works, as it is stated (Devarim 25:4): "You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing." In order to separate the grains from the ears and the chaff, they would lead an ox, which is a heavy animal, back and forth over the ears. This action is called threshing (dayish), that is, trampling and pressing down in order to extract the grains from the ears and the chaff. The Torah commanded not to muzzle the ox's mouth while it is threshing, because the smell of the grain rises in its nostrils and it longs to eat it, and when it tries to eat it encounters the muzzle, and its eyes pine with distress. It is not proper that the ox should work for our sake and we not share with it the benefit that grows from its work. And although the Torah wrote "ox," the intent is not to exclude other kinds of animals, but rather to give an example of an animal that works for us with foodstuffs. Therefore, all domestic and wild animals that work with produce of the ground, whether attached or detached, must be allowed to eat from it. This includes the prohibition of preventing a donkey from eating from the grain that it carries on its back. However, if the food with which it works could cause it intestinal upset and suffering, one may prevent it from eating it, for muzzling it is for its benefit, so that it will not suffer (Rambam, Hilkhot Sekhirut 13:1-3). If the owner of the ox wishes to spare the wheat, he may tie a basket containing ears of a cheap type of wheat to the ox's head, so that it may eat from them while it threshes, for the prohibition is to cause it distress, and in this way it is not distressed (ibid. 13:6).

Another law relating to tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim is the permission to milk cows full of milk on Shabbat. Although milking is forbidden by Torah law because of the melakha of 'threshing' (dash), since if they are not milked they will suffer greatly, the Sages permitted transgressing a rabbinic prohibition in order to ease their suffering. The simple way is to ask a non-Jew to do the milking, and if there is no non-Jew there who is willing to do so, a Jew may milk the milk so that it goes to waste, for in this manner the milking involves no Torah prohibition (Peninei Halakha, Shabbat 20:4).

A person who owns domestic or wild animals is obligated to provide for their food, and he is forbidden to eat before giving them their food. The Sages learned this (Gittin 62a) from what is stated (Devarim 11:15): "And I will give grass in your field for your cattle," and only afterwards, "and you shall eat and be satisfied."2

The reason for the prohibition is simple: since domesticated animals cannot provide for their own food, if their owners forget to give them food, they will suffer. In addition, since these animals work for man or produce milk for him, it is proper that he repay them as they deserve and provide for their food. Therefore, their owners must supply their food at fixed times. And so that they do not come to forget, it was established that a person should give them their food before his own.

The main prohibition concerns domestic and wild animals that are unable to find food for themselves, such as animals kept in pens, chickens in coops and a parrot in a cage, toward which compassion is great. But dogs and cats, which sometimes roam outside, since in a pinch they can survive on what they find outside, there is no prohibition for their owners to eat before giving them food. Nevertheless, it is a midat ḥasidut for their owners to give them their food first, before they eat. For although in a pinch they can manage on their own, since they have become domesticated it is difficult for them to find their food, and it is proper to have compassion on them. Furthermore, they are useful to man, for the cat preys on mice and snakes, and the dog is loyal to its owner and guards his house, and therefore it is proper to reward them for their service (She'ilat Ya'avetz 1:17).

The Sages said that a person should not bring an animal into his possession unless he knows that he will be able to feed it properly (Yerushalmi Ketubot 4:8). The Sages further said that God tested the leaders of Israel according to their behavior toward animals: at first Moshe Rabbeinu and King David were shepherds, and after the Holy One, blessed be He, saw that they managed their flocks with kindness and compassion and provided for their food, He chose them to be leaders of Israel (Shemot Rabba 2:2).

notes_en.en:
According to most poskim, the prohibition is rabbinic, and the proof from the verse is an asmakhta (a textual support). So wrote Responsa Shvut Ya'akov 3:13, and the Sdei Ḥemed, Kelalim 1:100. However, according to the Maharam of Rothenburg (4:302) and Magen Avraham (271:12), the prohibition is from the Torah. By contrast, from the wording of the Rambam in Hilkhot Avadim 9:8 it seems that it is a midat ḥasidut. And see BHL 167:6, s.v. 'U-mi-kol makom.'
Some say that only a full meal is forbidden to eat before feeding the animals, but tasting is permitted (Baḥ and Taz 167:7), and some say that even tasting a small taste at the beginning of the meal is forbidden beforehand (Shvut Ya'akov 3:13; Birkei Yosef 167:5). Drinking water is permitted according to all opinions.

sections.title_en: The Basis of the Permission for Human Needs
sections.body_en:
A person is permitted to cause suffering to animals for the sake of his livelihood, his dignity and his enjoyment, for example, to load burdens on them and to beat them so that they will walk, or to ride horses and guide them with a bridle that hurts their mouths, and to urge them on by lashing them with a whip and digging the spurs of his boots into their bodies. Just as a person exerts himself, sweats and endures indignity for the sake of his livelihood, so too his animal shares the burden with him, and since its stature and sensitivity are lesser, it can be subjected to harder and more painful work.

Not only that, but just as human beings are sometimes willing to bear very great suffering for the sake of their dignity and their faith, so, and even more so, it is sometimes permitted to cause suffering to animals for the sake of the dignity and faith of human beings. For example, after the death of a king, in his honor they would burn all his belongings so that other people would not use them, and this included hamstringing his horses, that is, cutting their legs above their hooves, so that they could not be used. And although this hamstringing causes them very great suffering, the honor of the king, which is the honor of all Israel, is more important (Avoda Zara 11a, Tosafot s.v. 'Okrin').

Likewise, it is stated before Israel's war against the kings of the north (Yehoshua 11:6): "And the Lord said to Yehoshua: Do not be afraid of them, for tomorrow at this time I will deliver them all up slain before Israel; you shall hamstring their horses and burn their chariots with fire." Thus he was commanded to hamstring the horses by cutting their legs above their hooves, so that they would limp on the stumps of their legs, as an object of abhorrence for having taken part in the war. And although it would have been possible to take them as spoil or to kill them, he was commanded to hamstring them in order to leave them maimed, and thereby to teach the enemies and Israel a lesson not to trust in horses (Radak, Abarbanel). And although the hamstringing caused the horses great suffering, we learn from here that for such a great moral need it is permitted to cause them suffering.

Likewise, we find that the Sages penalized one who went to trade on a market day dedicated to idolatry, that everything he bought there must be destroyed, and if he bought animals, their legs are cut above the hooves so that he cannot benefit from them. And although this involves tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim, they decreed to do so in order to distance Israel from idolatry (Avoda Zara 13a, Tosafot s.v. 'Amar Abaye').

Likewise, Rabbi Yehuda permitted selling a white rooster to a non-Jew, and so that he could not use it for idolatry, he should cut off its toe. Thus, for the sake of monetary profit they permitted causing it suffering by cutting off a toe (Mishna Avoda Zara 13b).

Likewise, the Sages enacted that if a person consecrated an animal to the Temple at a time when the Temple is destroyed, then, so as not to come to a mishap of misusing consecrated property by using the animal, it is placed in a closed place so that it dies there of hunger. They did not suggest slaughtering it and thereby reducing its suffering, lest people mistakenly eat its meat. Nor did they suggest killing it in another way, so as not to appear to be inflicting a blemish on consecrated animals (Avoda Zara 13b). Thus, for the sake of human beings, so that they not come to error, they ruled to cause an animal suffering by putting it to death through hunger (Ramban ibid. However, hamstringing causes more suffering – Rabbi Akiva Eiger, Avoda Zara 13a).

Likewise, we find that an elderly person for whom it is beneath his dignity to unload a donkey's burden is exempt from the mitzva even though the donkey is suffering and lying under its burden. Thus, a person's dignity takes precedence over tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim (Nimukei Yosef on Bava Metzia 32b).

sections.title_en: When It Is Forbidden to Cause Suffering
sections.body_en:
As we have learned, it is permitted to cause suffering to animals for the sake of a person's livelihood and dignity, but without a need it is forbidden to cause suffering to animals. Therefore, a person who enjoys beating and tormenting an animal is forbidden to do so, since there is no real need in this other than his evil desire to cause suffering to animals.

And even if cruel people come and are willing to pay a dog's owner a very high price so that he agrees to give them his dog so that they can torture it, he is forbidden to give them his dog for any fortune. For there is no need in this torture other than cruelty, which is forbidden by the Torah. Likewise, an irritable person who is in a bad mood is forbidden to beat an animal. And even if it is claimed that beating it helps him calm his nerves – it is forbidden by the Torah (Igrot Moshe EH 4:92; this also emerges from the definition of the Ḥatam Sofer, Bava Metzia 32b).

Following from this, it is not proper for a person to hunt wild animals and birds for sport and amusement, because the permission to kill animals for their meat or hides falls under the category of a necessity that is not to be condemned, and it is not proper to kill them for amusement and sport. It is not proper for Jews to enjoy this, for the trait of Israel is that they are compassionate (Yevamot 79a). Those mentioned in the Torah as hunters, Nimrod and Esav, were wicked people who enjoyed the cruelty of hunting (Or Zaru'a; Rema OḤ 316:2; Noda Bi-Yehuda, second edition, YD 10).3

However, there is no prohibition to catch fish with a fishing rod for enjoyment when the intention is to eat them, since in two respects this has an advantage over hunting. First, one intends to eat the fish that come up on the hook, so this involves a real benefit and not cruelty for its own sake, whereas the meat of animals and birds that were hunted is generally forbidden to Jews to eat. Second, fish are less developed than mammals and feel less pain and suffering, and therefore fishing is accompanied by fewer feelings of cruelty. But it is not proper to catch fish with a rod for enjoyment with the intention of returning them to the water afterwards, for in this way the enjoyment involves suffering, and although fish are not developed and their suffering is very slight (above, note 1), le-khatḥila it is better not to wound them without the intention of eating them.4

notes_en.en: Accordingly, my teacher and rabbi, Rav Shaul Yisraeli zt"l, ruled that one should not advertise hunting trips, so as not to take part in the transgression of these acts of cruelty (Be-mar'eh Ha-bazak 2:59). Meat obtained by hunting is generally forbidden to Jews to eat, for if the animal dies from the shot, it is certainly forbidden, since it was not slaughtered according to halakha. And even when the hunter's shot only wounds it, in most cases it will be considered a tereifa, whose meat is forbidden to eat.

In Ḥevel Naḥalato 10:37, he permitted fishing for enjoyment, because there is a human need in it, to calm a person, and in addition, since the fish is less developed, it is not clear to what extent it suffers from the hook stuck in its mouth. On the other hand, my friend Rav Ehud Aḥituv forbade fishing for enjoyment without the intention to eat, because of tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim (Emunat Itekha 86).

sections.body_en:
The attitude toward the life of animals differs from the attitude toward human life. Human life is holy, because man was created in the image of God, and the Holy One, blessed be He, breathed into him a living soul and placed upon him the responsibility for repairing the world, and every moment that the Divine soul dwells within him is more precious than fine gold, and under no circumstances may his life be shortened. Even if he is suffering from a severe illness, it is forbidden to kill him. However, the life of animals is not so precious, and therefore the mitzva is not to cause them suffering, but there is no mitzva to preserve their lives. Therefore, a person who has a cat or a dog that is suffering from a terminal illness or was injured in an accident, and is in agony with no chance of recovery – it is preferable that he put it to death in a painless way in order to spare it suffering.

Moreover, animal welfare ("tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim") organizations that have in their possession dogs and cats that no one wants may put them to death. Similarly, a person who has a dog and finds it difficult to continue feeding it, so that he is causing it suffering, and there is no one who wants to take it, may put it to death without suffering (Maharshal, Yam Shel Shlomo, Bava Kamma 10:37). It is true that we have learned that the Sages warned that a person should not bring an animal into his possession unless he knows that he will be able to feed it properly (Yerushalmi Ketubot 4:8). But if he erred and thought he would be able to support it and then realized that it is difficult for him, he is not bound to the animal to support it until the end of its life, and he may put it to death in order to spare it suffering, so that it does not die of hunger.

Sometimes there is an economic necessity to kill animals. For example, the owner of a fishpond must market the fish at certain times, according to market demand. And when the fish grow later or earlier than expected, he may be left with a pond full of fish and no buyers. Le-khatḥila, of course, one should look for a way to market the fish and not kill them for nothing. But if no solution is found, the owner of the fish is not obligated to continue spending money on feeding them, and he may kill them.

Likewise, there are chicks and chickens for which there is no demand, because the cost of caring for them is higher than the price the breeders could get for them, and then it is permitted to kill them, for the breeders are not bound to feed them without making an economic profit from it (see above 13:8).5

notes_en.en: The books 'Tza'ar Ba'alei Ḥayim' (2:2) and 'Nefesh Kol Ḥai' (5:1) wrote that the poskim disagree whether there is a prohibition to kill animals. Some say that the prohibition of tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim applies while they are alive, but there is no prohibition of tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim when killing them (Taz YD 116:6; Noda Bi-Yehuda, second edition, YD 10; Avodat Ha-Gershuni 13). However, they too would agree that if there is some benefit from them, killing them involves the prohibition of bal tashḥit (wanton destruction). Others say that the prohibition of tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim also includes a prohibition to kill them, and consequently it is permitted to kill them only for the sake of livelihood or dignity, just as it is permitted to cause them suffering (so they learned from the Rambam, Guide for the Perplexed 3:48; Ḥinukh 451, Radbaz and Ginat Veradim, on the reason for sheḥita; and so wrote the Maharsham 4:140). However, it seems that there is no need to say that there is a disagreement here, for all agree that the more prolonged their suffering, the greater the prohibition, and therefore the main issue of tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim is while they are alive, and only for a great need can it be permitted. On the other hand, all can agree that killing involves a certain suffering, even from the mere fact that they will not be able to go on living, and therefore without any need it is forbidden to kill them. Not only that, but when the intention is to eat their meat, the Torah commanded us to be doubly careful not to cause them suffering, and therefore it commanded sheḥita.

sections.body_en:
There are intermediate situations in which a person has a certain need whose fulfillment involves causing suffering to an animal, and the question is whether this is a real need that justifies causing suffering. The principle is that as long as the suffering is not caused out of cruelty but for the benefit of man, there is no prohibition. However, since it is not a clear-cut need, le-khatḥila, when possible, it is proper to avoid it. And the more the matter causes suffering to the animal, and the less necessary it is for man, the more proper it is to avoid it. People's understanding and custom are what determine the extent of the need for man, as well as the severity of the suffering for the animal, and accordingly one must determine when it is proper to refrain, or even to forbid.

For example, according to the letter of the law it is permitted to pluck feathers from live geese in order to make quills from them, but since plucking the feathers causes them great suffering, and it is possible to take feathers from slaughtered geese, it is proper to refrain from this (Terumat Ha-deshen; Rema EH 5:14).

Similarly, one should be careful not to pluck the feathers of a bird's neck in order to clear the place of sheḥita, so as not to cause it suffering for nothing; but when the slaughterer is not expert in his craft and needs this in order to be able to slaughter properly – it is permitted (Or Zaru'a; Rema YD 24:8).

Similarly, people are permitted to cut a dog's ears or tail so that it will look more attractive in their eyes, since this is done for the benefit of the person who enjoys his dog's beauty, and not out of cruelty. Nevertheless, from the standpoint of the trait of compassion, it is preferable not to cause them suffering. Similarly regarding a parrot: according to the law it is permitted to cut its tongue a little so that it will be able to utter words, for this gives pleasure to its owner, but le-khatḥila it is preferable to have compassion on it and refrain from this. However, it seems that if, as a result of refraining from the act that causes suffering to the dog or parrot, the owner would not want to raise it, then from his standpoint it is a real need, and therefore he may le-khatḥila perform the painful act on it – just as a person himself is willing to pay money and undergo operations in order to beautify himself.

It is permitted le-khatḥila to train animals with training that involves light blows. Even when the training involves harsh blows it is permitted, but it is a midat ḥasidut to refrain from this. And if without this the animal would not be of use and would presumably be put to death, it is permitted le-khatḥila.

According to the letter of the law it is permitted to hunt animals in order to make coats and wallets from their hides, but from the standpoint of midat ḥasidut it is proper to be stringent. In the past, many were not stringent about this, because man was forced to use the hides of animals to keep his body warm with coats and blankets. But today, when we know how to produce coats and blankets from synthetic materials, it is a midat ḥasidut not to hunt animals solely in order to use their hides (see Mayim Ḥayim 2:50, by Rav Ḥayim David Halevi).

sections.title_en: Methods of Raising Animals and Poultry for Food
sections.body_en:
The rule is that whatever a person does for his benefit and not for the sake of cruelty is permitted, and therefore it is permitted to raise chickens and calves for meat in great density in order to save on the costs of raising them. Likewise, it is permitted to raise laying hens and dairy cows in great density. Just as a person causes himself discomfort by working and living in crowded places in order to save costs, all the more so is he permitted to crowd animals in order to save costs.

However, some are inclined to say that when it involves great and terrible suffering, it is forbidden. For the permission to cause animals very great suffering, such as cutting the horses' legs above their hooves, is a rare permission for a special need, for the honor of the kingdom or for uprooting idolatry. But it is forbidden to cause them great suffering regularly and systematically for the sake of livelihood. Others are inclined to say that whatever is for the sake of livelihood, it is permitted to cause them even very great suffering. In practice, however, the questions are generally not about the principle; rather, the debate is whether this is indeed very great suffering, for by the nature of things, raising animals and feeding them for meat, milk and eggs does not involve very great suffering.6

Here is an example of such a question: naturally, hens lay eggs from the time they reach the age of six months until they reach the age of twenty months, and then they are slaughtered. It is possible to lengthen the egg-laying period by starving them in the fifteenth month for about ten days, whereupon their feathers fall out, and afterwards, when they return to eating, their strength returns, their feathers grow back, and they are able to lay eggs until they are twenty-eight months old. The question is whether it is permitted to starve them and cause them suffering for this purpose. Some forbid it, because it is permitted to cause animals suffering for the sake of livelihood only with ordinary suffering, but there is no permission to cause them great suffering for the sake of livelihood, for that is already considered forbidden cruelty (Shevet Ha-levi 2:7). According to many, this method of raising is permitted, since it is done for the benefit of the farm, and that is the purpose for which the birds are raised. In addition, in the long term the starving adds to their health, as evidenced by the fact that they live longer, and even human beings would be willing to go hungry for ten days in order to lengthen their lives. So wrote Rav Goldberg, the rabbi of Kfar Pines ('Ha-aretz U-mitzvoteha'; and so it was ruled in Minḥat Yitzḥak 6:145). In practice, it seems one may be lenient, both from reasoning and because in these matters there is an advantage to the rabbis of the moshavim, who are in the position of 'mara de-atra' (the local rabbinic authority), for they are intimately familiar with the methods of raising cattle and poultry, and know how to weigh the benefit to the farmers against the suffering of the animals. By contrast, one who is not familiar with the methods of raising poultry and calves is sometimes shocked to see them, and he is to some extent like a city-dweller who comes to a remote village and sees people living in huts without electricity and water, as their ancestors did for generations, and thinks that their whole lives are filled with sorrow and suffering without any contentment or joy.

However, there is room to say that along with the rise in the standard of living of human beings, morally and economically, the concept of 'tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim' may also change. And just as in the past certain things were not considered to cause suffering to people and today they are considered to cause suffering, so in parallel it is possible that things that were not perceived in the past as great and terrible suffering for animals will be perceived as great and terrible suffering, which it is forbidden to inflict on them systematically for the sake of livelihood. As a result, the number of people who abstain from eating the meat of animals raised in a manner that causes suffering, according to their understanding, will increase. This position can also gradually influence the general public, whose representatives will weigh the full range of values and public pressures and enact laws that on the one hand will reduce the suffering of the cattle and poultry raised for the food industry, and on the other hand will take into account the general public, and especially the poor, so as not to raise the price of food for them excessively. In a less good situation, under the pressure of animal rights activists, laws will be enacted that do not take the poor into account and do not weigh the full range of values, and it will be necessary to amend and balance them.7

notes_en.en: Rav Eliyahu Klatzkin, in Imrei Shefer 34, forbade causing animals great suffering for the needs of livelihood, and so wrote the Yad Ha-levi, YD 196. Most poskim permitted it, among them Yam Shel Shlomo, Bava Kamma 10:37; Shvut Ya'akov 3:71; Ḥatam Sofer, Bava Metzia 32b; Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav, Hilkhot Tza'ar Ba'alei Ḥayim 4; Da'at Kedoshim YD 24:12. In Shevet Ha-levi 2:7 he introduced a novel view that there are three levels: a) slight suffering, which is rabbinically forbidden; b) great suffering, which is forbidden by the Torah but permitted for the needs of livelihood, and this is the ordinary suffering that was permitted; c) very great suffering, which is considered cruelty and is forbidden even for the needs of livelihood. In my humble opinion, the third level too is permitted, just as they permitted hamstringing horses (as explained in halakha 5), and there is no greater suffering than that. But this permission is intended for special cases and not as systematic conduct. However, when the purpose is cruelty, even ordinary suffering is forbidden, as explained in halakha 6.

An example of this is the debate over force-feeding geese. In the past, force-feeding was considered acceptable suffering for the needs of livelihood. We also learned incidentally from a discussion in the laws of Shabbat (Shabbat 155b) that they would stuff camels, that is, push food into their throats by force to a place from which they could not regurgitate it, so that they would be able to travel in the desert for many days without eating. Similarly, they would stuff calves and force-feed chickens in order to fatten them, that is, forcibly push the food into their throats to a place from which they could not regurgitate it (Beitza 29b). Likewise, they would force-feed geese in order to fatten them, to the point that the geese no longer knew how to eat by themselves unless the food was pushed into their throats, and it was permitted to ask a non-Jew to force-feed them on Shabbat so that they would not suffer from hunger (Responsa of the Rema 79). However, a problem arose: as a result of forcibly pushing the food into their throats, the gullet was injured, and there was a concern that the goose had become a tereifa. Some permitted the geese after checking the gullet (Rema YD 33:9, and many others), and some forbade them, because they may have become tereifa without this being seen in the check of the gullet (Baḥ and many others).
In recent generations force-feeding was refined, and instead of doing it by hand they began to use machines. They also found that in order to enlarge the liver, it is good to force-feed the goose with corn and to restrict the goose's movement; in this way the liver is enlarged to ten times its normal size. Some hold that in this manner the goose's suffering is greater, because it is force-fed a larger quantity; in addition, the dry corn increases the risk of injuring the gullet and rendering it tereifa. On the other hand, some hold that this involves no more suffering than in the past. Not only that, but recently the method was refined, and the geese were force-fed a wet corn mash that is introduced into the stomach through a thin tube, in a way that does not burden it during the force-feeding and also reduces the risk of it becoming tereifa. Still, many claim that enlarging the liver to ten times its size causes the goose great suffering and difficulty breathing and walking. As for the halakha, some inclined to forbid it because of tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim (Rav Ya'akov Epstein in Ḥevel Naḥalato 9:26), and some say there is no prohibition in it (Rav Itai Elitzur in 'Teḥumin' 24; Rav Pinḥas Toledano, Brit Shalom, vol. 2, ḤM 7). According to Rav Ya'akov Ariel shlit"a, there is no prohibition in it, but it is not mehudar (of the highest standard), and therefore the hekhsher they gave for goose liver is kasher and not ḥalak (glatt). In practice, as a result of the fierce struggles of animal welfare organizations against goose farmers, in quite a few countries a law was enacted forbidding the force-feeding of geese. In the State of Israel, public representatives tried to establish with the goose farmers an intermediate framework that would allow force-feeding of geese to continue in conditions more comfortable for the geese, but the High Court of Justice decided to accept the position of the animal welfare organizations and absolutely forbade the force-feeding of geese in Israel.

sections.body_en:
It is permitted, and even a mitzva, to conduct scientific experiments on animals in order to understand diseases and find cures for human beings. Even when the experiments involve great suffering, there is no prohibition, since they are done for a benefit and not for the sake of cruelty. Even from the standpoint of midat ḥasidut one should not refrain from them, since through them it is possible to find a cure for the illnesses of many people, and the supreme moral obligation is to care for the life and health of human beings (see Shvut Ya'akov 3:71; Seridei Esh 3:7). Not only that, but human beings too are willing to afflict themselves and endanger their lives in order to save their children or friends and heal them, and the more people the danger concerns, the more people are willing to undergo severe suffering and enter into dangers in order to save their fellows. All the more so is a person permitted to cause suffering to animals in his possession in order to find a cure for human diseases.

However, every experiment must be examined on its own merits as to whether it is necessary to perform it. Likewise, when it can be tested on different animals, it is preferable to perform it on the lower species. For example, an experiment that can be conducted on monkeys or on mice – it is preferable to conduct it on mice, because their nervous system and brain are less developed, and they feel less pain and suffering. By contrast, monkeys are so developed that it is evident when they are happy and content or sad and in pain, and therefore one must be more careful not to cause them suffering (above, note 1, paragraph 1). Even after it has been decided that there is a vital need to conduct research on animals, one must make an effort to minimize their suffering. For example, if it involves an operation, one should try to perform it under anesthesia. And if, as a result of the research, their bodies are damaged, they should be put to death with an easy death in order to spare them suffering (Tzitz Eliezer 14:68).

According to the letter of the law, high-school students are permitted to perform experiments on insects, to check at what heat they manage to survive and at what heat they die, at what cold they survive and at what cold they die. And although all these experiments have already been performed, there is a certain benefit in the students becoming accustomed to performing experiments. In addition, the main prohibition of tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim applies to animals that help man and have a certain consciousness, and not to insects, whose nervous system is immeasurably inferior. However, since these experiments have no scientific benefit, and it is also not clear that these students will go on to develop as scientists whom it is important to accustom to such experiments, it is preferable that they perform experiments that do not cause suffering to animals, for it is proper to have compassion on all creatures, as it is stated (Tehillim 145:9): "And His compassion is over all His works."

It is forbidden to raise a pet that causes distress to the neighbors. Therefore it is forbidden to raise a vicious dog, that is, a dog that might frighten people or children passing in the street next to the dog's yard. Likewise, it is forbidden to raise a dog that barks and makes noise and distresses the neighbors and disturbs their rest. Even when it is a trained dog, regarding which there is no concern that it will attack people, and it does not disturb the neighbors' rest with its barking – as long as passersby do not know that it is trained and may be frightened when it barks at them, it is forbidden to raise it. Only if passersby are not afraid of it, for example because it is tied with iron chains or is in a fenced-in place, so that it is evident to all that it cannot attack, is it permitted to raise it. In isolated places, where there is a security need for this, it is permitted to release frightening dogs at night to guard the community, provided that they pose no danger to the residents of the community. And dogs that are not frightening at all, either because of their great friendliness or because the local people are accustomed to these dogs, need not be tied (Bava Kamma 79b-80a; SA ḤM 409:3).

A person who sees a snake or a scorpion in a place where people walk is commanded to kill it, so that it does not kill a person. Likewise, it is a mitzva to kill a lion, wolf or leopard roaming in inhabited areas, so that it does not harm people. However, when people raise a predatory animal or a venomous snake in a place where they are well guarded, so that they cannot harm anyone, they should not be harmed. But if the owner is negligent in guarding them and they pose a danger, their owner is obligated to kill them, and if he does not do so, anyone may kill them in order to save himself and the public from the danger they pose (Tosafot, Bava Kamma 16b, s.v. 'Rabbi,' according to the explanation of Rabbeinu Tam; Noda Bi-Yehuda, second edition, YD 10).

A person is permitted to kill mice and rats that damage his fields or have entered his house (Mishna Mo'ed Katan 6b).

It is permitted to exterminate insects and other pests from fields and the house, since they harm man (Radbaz 2:727). In addition, the main prohibition of tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim does not apply to lower animals, whose nervous system and brain are not developed and whose sensation of pain and suffering is very weak. And although it is a midat ḥasidut to refrain from harming any living creature, in order to prevent damage it is permitted to kill them, and there is no aspect of piety in refraining from this.

Likewise, it is permitted to kill ants, flies and other creeping creatures that have entered the house and interfere with its cleanliness. And although it is a midat ḥasidut to be careful not to harm any living creature, even if it is of a lower species, when it disturbs a person, even from the standpoint of midat ḥasidut it is permitted to kill it, because the cleanliness of a person's home and his dignity are more important.8

notes_en.en:
As we learned above in halakha 1, rule 2, the more an animal is capable of feeling its pain, the more careful one must be not to cause it suffering. Therefore, in a time of need one need not be concerned about the suffering of insects and pests, whose nervous system and brain are extremely inferior. Furthermore, the She'ilat Ya'avetz (1:110) wrote that the Torah prohibition of tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim applies only to domestic and wild animals that serve man, and therefore he permitted killing harmful vermin and creeping creatures without restriction. And according to the Noda Bi-Yehuda (second edition, YD 10), there is no prohibition of tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim in killing an animal, but only when one causes it suffering while it is alive.
Some wrote that it is preferable to kill harmful animals, such as mice, indirectly by means of poison or a trap and not with one's own hands, so as not to become accustomed to cruelty (Igrot Moshe ḤM 2:47). It seems that if the mouse is caught in glue, it is preferable to have pity on it and kill it by hand with a blow or by drowning it in water, rather than leaving it to die in agony.

sections.body_en:
It is forbidden to hold or watch bullfighting spectacles, since animals are made to suffer in them, and in addition human life is endangered in them. First, the bulls are starved so that they will be agitated; afterwards, in the arena, the bullfighter, who is called a matador, waves a red cloth before the bull in order to agitate and anger it until it comes to attack him. And if the bull does not want to fight, the matador stabs it until it gets up and becomes enraged. Finally, when the bull furiously attacks the matador who angered it, the matador must nimbly evade the bull and stab it to death. Then the crowd screams and roars and cheers the heroic matador. On rare occasions, it happens that the bull is quicker than the matador, and then the matador is killed or injured. In such a case, according to halakha, the bull bears no guilt at all; for although generally an ox that killed a person must be put to death, here, where the matador provoked it to attack him, the ox is exempt from punishment (Bava Kamma 39a; Rambam, Hilkhot Nizkei Mamon 6:5).

In the Roman period these cruel spectacles were the popular entertainment. As a prelude, they would set dogs upon other animals and watch with pleasure how the animals tore each other apart. And every time an animal succeeded in overpowering its fellow and tearing its throat, the spectators would exult and cheer loudly. Afterwards, they would bring in slaves and captives to fight the beasts of prey, and even when the beast succeeded in killing the person, the people would exult and cheer loudly. Many Jews who fell into Roman captivity were also killed in this way. To our great shame, there were Jews who were drawn after the dominant culture and wanted to watch these cruel spectacles; presumably they did so when the captives were from another nation. Against this the Sages stood up and ruled that it is forbidden to go to these wicked spectacles, and they applied to this the verse (Tehillim 1:1): "Happy is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked, nor stood in the way of sinners" – happy is he who has not gone to the theaters, circuses and stadiums of the gentiles, in which cruel spectacles of the murder of slaves and of tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim are held amid revelry and mockery (Avoda Zara 18b). In our times we have merited to advance to a situation in which spectacles in which human beings are murdered are no longer held, but the bullfighting spectacle is also forbidden, because of tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim and the endangerment of human life.

Likewise, it is forbidden to train roosters to fight one another and kill one another. And anyone who buys a ticket to such spectacles becomes a partner in a transgression and causes himself a moral blemish in the trait of compassion.9

notes_en.en: Human beings too box and wrestle and strike one another, as amateurs or professionals, but it seems that as long as there is no peace in the whole world, there is a benefit for people in this, for the purpose of learning self-defense and warfare, and therefore in all nations and armies it has been customary to train young people and soldiers for hand-to-hand combat (see II Shmuel 2:14; Orot Ha-teḥiya 34). From this need, sports related to it developed, and since these are competitions full of tension, interest in them is great. Some hold that through these competitions violence is actually reduced, since it is given a controlled outlet, and some hold the opposite, that these competitions encourage violence. In practice, it seems that it is not proper to enjoy those sports that hold competitions in which the cruelty is especially prominent or the injuries are severe, such as professional boxing. And from here to animals: just as fighters and police officers were trained, so it was customary to train horses for the needs of war and law enforcement, and in consequence horse races were held, and it is permitted to watch them (Mahari Bruna 71). But it is forbidden to hold fights in which animals are killed and injured, and it is also forbidden to encourage them by watching. For the animals derive no sporting benefit from this, and the main enjoyment that people have from them involves cruelty and suffering; and so it is explained in Yeḥaveh Da'at 3:66.

sections.body_en:
It is permitted to keep pets such as a dog, cat and parrot. It is true that the Sages forbade a Jew to trade in non-kosher animals, that is, animals whose meat is not kosher for eating. But the prohibition concerns animals whose meat non-Jews are accustomed to eat, and they decreed not to trade in them lest, because they are commonly in the possession of a Jew, he come to eat their meat. But there is no prohibition regarding non-kosher animals whose meat people are not accustomed to eat, and it is permitted to trade in them and to raise them for amusement and affection (Beit Yosef YD 117; Birkei Yosef 2). Some do claim that since these animals are called tamei (impure), it is not proper to bring them into the house. However, this reasoning is not mentioned in the books of the poskim. These animals are called tamei because they are forbidden to eat and one who eats their meat defiles himself, but this does not mean that their traits are so flawed that one who raises them might be harmed in his soul. On the contrary, every animal has a good and special trait of its own, and the Sages praised even species of non-kosher animals, and noted the loyalty of the dog and the modesty of the cat; therefore it is permitted to keep pets.

However, when the pet causes distress to one of the family members – it is forbidden to keep it. Therefore, one who has a dog that habitually frightens visitors to his home must send it for training, so that the dog will learn to stop this and its owner will be able to host guests with proper respect (Shabbat 63a-b).

The Sages said that a person should not bring an animal into his possession unless he knows that he will be able to provide it with proper food (Yerushalmi Ketubot 4:8). This includes being able to provide a suitable kennel or cage for it, as well as being able to clean its place as needed, and seeing to its vaccination if this is necessary.

When his animal becomes ill, its owner must care for it in the accepted way. When its illness is terminal and it is suffering, it is better to put it to death in order to ease its suffering. A person who erred and found that he is in fact unable to care for his animal should try to find it another owner who will care for it, and if he does not find one, he is not obligated to keep it and support it, and when necessary he may put it to death in order to minimize its suffering (above, section 7).

It is permitted to feed fish in an aquarium with live worms without being concerned about the suffering of the worms, because the prohibition of tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim applies specifically when causing them suffering for nothing, but for a need it is permitted. In addition, the prohibition of tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim concerns animals with a certain consciousness, which feel their suffering more, whereas regarding animals of a lower species the main prohibition is not to destroy them for nothing (above, halakha 1, the second rule). Likewise, one who has a need to raise a snake is permitted to feed the snake mice. And although the mouse is more developed than the snake, since there is a human need in this, it is permitted.

It is permitted, and even has value, to maintain a zoo, because the animals in the zoo receive good food, and there is benefit and value in this for human beings, who can see them and learn about them (Yabi'a Omer 4, OḤ 20).

It is permitted to conduct psychological therapy with the help of animals, whereby through relating to the animal, such as a dog, the patient learns to be considerate of others; and through taking responsibility for feeding it and cleaning and arranging its place, he strengthens his confidence and responsibility. It is true that sometimes patients who do not know how to relate properly to others may at first frighten the animal, or get angry at it, or hold it too tightly; nevertheless, this is permitted le-khatḥila, since it is an important need, and on the other hand there is no intention to cause suffering to the animal, but rather to turn the patient into a person capable of caring for and being good to the animal.

The aim of creation is to add life to the world, as it is stated after the creation of the fish and birds (Bereishit 1:22): "And God blessed them, saying: Be fruitful and multiply." Following from this, the Torah forbade the act of castration, that is, an act that damages one of the reproductive organs of a person or of a domestic animal, wild animal or bird. Anyone who castrates one of them transgresses a Torah prohibition whose punishment is lashes (Vayikra 22:24; SA EH 5:11).

The Torah prohibition of castration was stated regarding males, whose reproductive organs are exposed and whom people were accustomed to castrate; but castration of females, according to most poskim, is rabbinically forbidden. Some say that castrating a female is also forbidden by the Torah, but that one does not receive lashes for castrating a female. On the other hand, some say that there is not even a rabbinic prohibition to castrate females, but since it is forbidden to cause them suffering, it is consequently forbidden to castrate them, for castration involves great pain; and if they are castrated without suffering, there is no prohibition.

Recently, animal welfare organizations have become aware of the problem of street cats, which, having no enemy to thin their population, have multiplied greatly, and the food thrown into the garbage bins is not sufficient for their sustenance, and they roam hungry and emaciated, wailing in distress and trying to sneak into houses to quiet their hunger. Some proposed to catch male cats, castrate them by cutting their sperm ducts, and mark them by cutting off part of their ear so that they will not mistakenly be caught a second time, until about eighty percent of the males are castrated. And since the great majority of them will be sterile, they will not be able to fertilize the females, and the cat population will decrease.

However, as we have learned, this is forbidden by the Torah. It is also forbidden to hire non-Jews to castrate the cats, because anything that is forbidden to a Jew by Torah prohibition, the Sages forbade a Jew to ask a non-Jew to do (SA EH 5:14). In addition, some hold that the descendants of Noaḥ too are forbidden to castrate animals, in which case it is forbidden by the Torah to ask them to castrate cats, for we were commanded not to cause a person to stumble in transgression. And according to most poskim it is rabbinically forbidden to castrate the females as well. Therefore, it may be suggested that from time to time tasty cat food containing contraceptive pills be scattered in the streets, and these pills will prevent ovulation and heat in the female cats, and in this way the cat population will decrease without the prohibition of castration.

This is also the correct advice for one who does not want his female dog to become pregnant: he should give her contraceptive pills. And although there is a concern that these pills may cause illnesses, this is the proper solution according to halakha. And if efforts are made, it will be possible to produce contraceptive pills for animals that do not cause illnesses, just as they succeeded in producing contraceptive pills for human beings that do not cause illnesses. In a pressing situation, since according to many the prohibition of castrating a female is rabbinic, a Jew may sterilize a female dog or cat by means of an injection or by blocking the fallopian tubes, because this is a method of 'gerama,' that is, an action that causes castration indirectly and after a time. Alternatively, a non-Jewish veterinarian may sterilize her surgically.10

notes_en.en:
It is forbidden to ask a non-Jew to castrate an animal, because according to most poskim the shevut (rabbinic prohibition) of amira le-akum (instructing a non-Jew) applies to all Torah prohibitions: just as a Jew is forbidden to ask a non-Jew to desecrate Shabbat for him, so he is forbidden to ask a non-Jew to do another prohibited act. The Ra'avad is indeed lenient, but most poskim are stringent. This is the view of the Rambam, Rosh, Nimukei Yosef, Rashba and Ran, and so it was ruled in SA EH 5:14 (see Peninei Halakha, Shevi'it 5, note 9).
In addition, we learned in Sanhedrin 56b and 57a that according to the Tanna of the school of Menashe and Rabbi Ḥidka, the descendants of Noaḥ are forbidden to castrate, as it is stated (Bereishit 9:7): "Swarm in the earth and multiply in it." According to the Sages, this is a blessing and not a commandment. Most Rishonim ruled like the Sages, and this is the view of the Rosh (Bava Metzia 7:6), Nimukei Yosef (Bava Metzia 53a), Beit Yosef (EH 5), and the Bi'ur Ha-Gra in the name of the poskim. However, according to the She'iltot (Emor, She'ilta 105), the descendants of Noaḥ too are forbidden to castrate, and this is also the view of the Semag (negative commandments 120) and Or Zaru'a (Bava Metzia, siman 286).
Regarding castration of a female: according to the Gra (EH 5:25), the prohibition is from the Torah but lashes are not given for it, and its source is the Torat Kohanim. According to most poskim the prohibition is rabbinic, because their reproductive organs are covered, and the main obligation of being fruitful and multiplying is upon males; and so it is implied by the wording of the Rambam (Hilkhot Issurei Bi'ah 16:11) and the Maggid Mishneh there. This is also the view of the Ramban and Rashba on Shabbat 111a. According to the Taz (EH 5:6), there is no prohibition of castration regarding females; rather, the Sages forbade castrating females only because of tza'ar ba'alei ḥayim. This is also the view of the Prisha (and only regarding a woman did he forbid it, because of "He did not create it to be a waste"). Responsa Lev Aryeh (2:34) wrote that according to this, if the animal is anesthetized and sterilized without pain, there is no prohibition. But in practice, since according to most poskim it is forbidden to castrate a female, it is difficult to permit castration of female animals even for the purpose of medical study. The book Nishmat Avraham (EH 5:9) wrote that this is what Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach told him. And my teacher and rabbi, Rav Avraham Shapira zt"l, told me likewise, that castration of a female should not be permitted, and that a solution of contraceptive pills should be found, and if there is no choice, it is even better to kill animals than to castrate them. End quote.
The convenient advice is to ask a non-Jewish veterinarian to sterilize a female: since castrating a female is rabbinically forbidden to a Jew, instructing a non-Jew is a 'shevut de-shevut' (a double rabbinic prohibition), and since even for the Torah prohibition of castrating a male there is no death penalty, one may be lenient le-khatḥila in a 'shevut de-shevut' of this prohibition (as explained in Peninei Halakha, Shevi'it 5, note 9; and see Shevet Ha-levi 6:204). In a pressing situation it seems one may be lenient and allow a Jew to sterilize a female by means of an injection, for this is sterilization by gerama (indirect causation), whose level is like a 'shevut de-shevut,' which is permitted when performed by a Jew for a great need. Likewise, it is possible to permit it by blocking the fallopian tubes in an indirect manner (and see Peninei Halakha, Simḥat Ha-bayit U-virkhato 7:5, note 8).

sections.body_en:
As we have learned (halakha 4), a person is obligated to provide for the food of the animals in his possession, but he is not obligated to provide for the food of ownerless animals. Therefore, one who sees hungry wild animals need not exert himself to supply them with food, for the mitzva of tzedaka was stated with regard to human beings and not with regard to animals. Therefore there is no obligation to save leftover food in order to give it to animals, but one who has compassion on wild animals and gives them some of his leftover food fulfills a mitzva thereby. For it is said of the Holy One, blessed be He: "And His compassion is over all His works," "You open Your hand and satisfy every living thing with favor" (Tehillim 145:9, 16), and a person is commanded to cleave to the attributes of the Holy One, blessed be He. And since there is a mitzva in this, even on Shabbat, which is meant for rest, one may exert oneself a little to put out leftover food for animals. This is on condition that they are hungry animals that have difficulty finding their food, such as dogs and cats. But for animals that manage on their own, such as bees for example, it is forbidden to exert oneself on Shabbat (SA OḤ 324:11; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 2-3; MB 31).

Likewise, one should try not to cause the extinction of any species of animal or plant. Recently, as a result of technological development, the human population has increased greatly, many forests have been cut down, fields have been cleared, and many species have been pushed out of their habitats and are in danger of extinction. So that no species will be lost from the world, it is proper that we try to minimize harm to animals, for every species that God created has a special value and role. As the Sages said (Shabbat 77b): "Of all that the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He did not create a single thing in vain." And they gave examples of various animals that seem useless, but in truth have various benefits, such as the preparation of medicines. The Sages further said that from every species a special praise rises to the Holy One, blessed be He, as is brought in 'Perek Shira.' If so, when a certain species is lost from the world, its completeness is, as it were, diminished, and the praise of the Holy One, blessed be He, is diminished. Therefore it is proper to assist associations that have set themselves the goal of protecting animal species so that they will not become extinct from the world. At the same time, when there is a conflict between the real needs of man and the needs and existence of animals – the needs of man prevail.
